title: Announcing Native Sandboxing in Ray | Anyscale
gist: Anyscale and Google built gVisor-based sandboxing natively into Ray (2.58+), representing isolated, untrusted-code execution environments as ordinary Ray Actors so agentic RL and coding-agent workloads can schedule them with Ray's existing autoscaling and fault tolerance, demonstrating scale to 100,000 sandboxes in 20 seconds on GKE and shipping a Harbor integration aimed squarely at the coding-agent evaluation market.

insights.claim: Agentic RL requires running large numbers of isolated environments executing model-generated code, and until now teams building these workloads on Ray had to either rely on a hosted sandbox provider or build and operate an entirely separate sandboxing control plane alongside their Ray cluster, duplicating scheduling, resource management, autoscaling, and fault tolerance.
insights.speaker: Philipp Moritz et al.
insights.so_what: Frames native Ray sandboxing as removing a duplicated infrastructure layer for any team running agentic RL -- directly relevant to assessing hosted sandbox providers' exposure to this workload segment.

insights.claim: The design principle is a clean division of labor -- 'Ray handles orchestration and scaling, gVisor handles isolation' -- implemented by representing each sandbox as an ordinary Ray Actor, so a sandbox automatically inherits Ray's existing placement, resource management, failure recovery, and autoscaling machinery instead of requiring a new abstraction.
insights.speaker: Philipp Moritz et al.
insights.so_what: A reusable architectural pattern: bolting a new resource type (isolated execution) onto an existing distributed runtime's actor model rather than building a parallel control plane.

insights.claim: On Google Kubernetes Engine, Ray Sandboxing has scaled to 100,000 gVisor sandboxes created in 20 seconds, distributed across thousands of nodes.
insights.speaker: Philipp Moritz et al.
insights.so_what: A concrete, aggressive scale benchmark aimed squarely at large-scale agentic RL workloads that continuously create and destroy environments as rollouts progress -- a capability metric worth comparing against hosted sandbox providers' published scale numbers.

insights.claim: gVisor was chosen as the initial sandbox runtime because it implements a substantial portion of the Linux system-call interface in userspace (adding an isolation boundary beyond ordinary containers), is OCI-compatible with standard container images, does not require exposing a Docker daemon or socket to the sandbox, and provides sub-second startup with low per-sandbox memory overhead.
insights.speaker: Philipp Moritz et al.
insights.so_what: Explains the specific technical properties (fast startup, low overhead, no daemon exposure) that make gVisor suitable as a fine-grained, dynamically-created distributed resource rather than a heavyweight VM-based isolation approach.

insights.claim: Ray Sandboxing is explicitly targeted at the existing ecosystem of RL frameworks already coordinating distributed training on Ray -- veRL, NeMo-RL, SLIME, MILES, and SkyRL -- positioning this as infrastructure meant to sit underneath the entire current Ray-based agentic RL stack rather than a standalone product.
insights.speaker: Philipp Moritz et al.
insights.so_what: Signals Anyscale is building sandboxing as connective infrastructure for an ecosystem of RL frameworks it doesn't own outright, similar to how Ray itself became the common substrate under multiple training frameworks.

insights.claim: Ray Sandboxing offers four distinct network isolation modes (none, public, host, and sandbox), letting teams tune the isolation-versus-connectivity tradeoff per sandbox -- e.g., fully isolated loopback-only for untrusted rollouts versus internet egress for sandboxes that need to call APIs or install packages.
insights.speaker: Philipp Moritz et al.

insights.claim: Ray Sandbox ships as a native backend for Harbor, a framework for evaluating coding agents such as Claude Code, OpenHands, and Codex CLI on benchmarks including SWE-Bench and Terminal-Bench, letting evaluation trials run under gVisor on the user's own Ray nodes with the task's network policy enforced by the sandbox; on a single 14-CPU dev VM, 8 trials at concurrency 4 completed with 8/8 reward, zero exceptions, in 3 minutes 2 seconds.
insights.speaker: Philipp Moritz et al.
insights.so_what: A concrete, near-term commercial wedge: Ray Sandboxing directly targets the fast-growing coding-agent benchmarking/evaluation market, not just RL training infrastructure.

insights.claim: GPU-backed sandboxes are explicitly on the roadmap, motivated by the expectation that workloads such as kernel generation and recursive self-improvement (RSI) will become increasingly important -- a forward-looking signal about where Anyscale expects agentic RL compute demand to move next.
insights.speaker: Philipp Moritz et al.
insights.so_what: Flags kernel-generation and self-improving-agent workloads as an anticipated growth area for sandboxed GPU compute, worth tracking against broader industry RSI/agentic-coding trends.

insights.claim: A planned REST API service would decouple sandbox access from requiring Ray as a dependency, enabling separate training and sandboxing clusters -- hinting at an eventual path to productizing sandboxing as a standalone service independent of the Ray runtime itself.
insights.speaker: Philipp Moritz et al.

insights.claim: The team explicitly states it wants to develop security configurations 'intended for workloads in which models may actively attempt to escape the sandbox,' an implicit acknowledgment that current agentic models are already being treated as adversarial actors against their own training/eval infrastructure, not merely untrusted-but-passive code.
insights.speaker: Philipp Moritz et al.
insights.so_what: A notable admission from an infrastructure vendor: the security model for agentic RL sandboxing must now assume active adversarial behavior from the models themselves, which has implications for how aggressively agentic RL and coding-agent training should be isolated going forward.
insights.quote: including configurations intended for workloads in which models may actively attempt to escape the sandbox
